newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Bonn deaf to fears about single currency.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bonn deaf to fears about single currency.

text.p: Fed up with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's relentless drive to unite Europe's currencies, Immo Wegner decided there was nothing left but to take matters into his own hands.

Like millions of Germans, the 48-year-old computer systems salesman was growing sick and tired worrying that new "euros" would some day displace the cherished deutschemarks in his pocket. So he began an advertising crusade to save the mark.

Wegner's one-man operation is just one of a flurry of small, disparate groups springing up in defence of the German currency -- a powerful symbol and guarantee of the country's famed post-World War Two stability and affluence.

All but ignored by the German media who dismiss them as the lunatic fringe, these groups reflect a growing fear among Germans that Europe's planned single currency will not match the fabled strength of the mark.

"Two-thirds of Germans are opposed to the euro and want to keep the deutschemark. Despite that, the government is pushing ahead with the plan regardless. I'm against a process that flouts the will of the majority," Wegner said.
THE MARK -- "MORE THAN JUST A CURRENCY"

For most Germans the deutschemark, introduced in 1948 in the chaotic aftermath of the war to replace the spent Reichsmark of the imperial and Nazi eras, is more than just a currency. It is a powerful source of national pride.
Yet for a country with few such symbols, Kohl's government and Germany's political establishment are determined to swap it for an untested pan-European currency to be called the euro.

"I voted for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) over the last years, but I don't feel represented anymore and I don't see an alternative among the other parties," said Wegner, who runs the Deutschemark Protection Group from his home in the southern town of Nieder-Olm.
Wegner likens his anti-euro sticker campaign, with slogans "D-mark -- yes," and "euro -- no," to the early anti-nuclear campaigners in style, if not in content.

Plots to foil Kohl's euro plans brew across Germany. Many, waged on Internet web sites and via newspaper advertisements, call for a referendum, a step Kohl has ruled out and for which there is no constitutional provision in Germany.
That is why many see their most effective weapon in legal challenges.
For a nation that was traumatised by hyper-inflation in the 1920s and 1930s, the mark's stability is so important that it is enshrined in the constitution.
LEGAL CHALLENGES

Former EU official Manfred Brunner, who quit Brussels in protest against the Maastricht Treaty, is the only person so far to succeed in challenging the 1992 pact in Germany's Federal Constitutional Court.
It ruled a year later that Germany could launch a single European currency only if it proved to be as stable as the mark and showed good prospects for future stability.
Others are also trying to take Bonn to court.

Klaus Peter Heim, a retired magazine editor, lists instances of cooking the books by countries wanting to join EMU. Wilhelm Noelling, a former Bundesbank central council member, wants to sue Bonn if the euro shows signs of disintegrating.
Brunner, a Munich-based lawyer, said in an interview: "If Bonn goes ahead with EMU next year, there will be flood of lawsuits."
Wegner tells Germans that the mark's 20 percent fall in value against the U.S. dollar since last year could be just the beginning of a downward spiral.
POLITICAL STONEWALLING
All Germany's main parties advocate a single currency, arguing it is needed to make Europe's postwar peace irreversible and regenerate its flagging economies.
They quickly denounce as a populist anyone who raises doubts about the euro.

However, a few mainstream politicians have proposed delaying the common currency project until countries wanting to join are economically fit enough -- a move euro-proponents say would spell its death.

Another anti-euro campaigner, investment magazine editor Bolko Hoffmann, launched the Pro D-Mark Initiative to support these politicians, notably state premiers Edmund Stoiber of Bavaria and Gerhard Schroeder of Lower Saxony, who is a favourite to stand against Kohl for the Social Democratic opposition in elections next year.
FEARS ECHOED ACROSS THE COUNTRY
While Kohl and his allies are adamant that Germany will launch the euro according to plan in 1999, surveys show the little support there ever was for it is waning.
A poll by the Forsa institute showed last month that 34 percent of Germans wanted the euro while 51 percent were opposed. The rest were unsure.

It found a large concentration of euro-opponents in formerly communist east Germany where, as one east Berliner put it seven years after the monetary union that set the stage for German reunification:
"East Germans were so pleased to get a convertible currency for once -- they're not in a hurry to give it up again."

Dissent may be strongest in the impoverished east, but anti-euro activists tend to be middle-aged, middle-class, conservative western Germans fearful that their life savings and fortunes will depreciate, according to Wegner.

"They don't want to lose what they worked so hard to achieve since the war," he said, citing hundreds of letters he has received from anxious Germans in response to a newspaper advertisement about his campaign.
